terms: department of health and human services
supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS SNAP consumer page (dhhs.nh.gov); NH EASY portal (nheasy.nh.gov)
supplements.heading: New Hampshire calls its program plainly "SNAP" — no distinctive local brand — and its self-service portal is NH EASY, run by DHHS's Bureau of Family Assistance
supplements.text: New Hampshire DHHS's own consumer materials use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive New Hampshire-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." New Hampshire's current self-service application portal is NH EASY (nheasy.nh.gov), administered by DHHS's Bureau of Family Assistance (BFA). Applicants can also apply by phone through Client Services (603-271-9700, or 1-800-852-3345 extension 9700, which will mail an application), by mail, or in person at a local DHHS District Office. New Hampshire also has a DHHS-partnered SNAP Outreach organization, the New Hampshire Food Bank, which assists with applications. New Hampshire's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DHHS's BFA through District Offices — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, and New Mexico packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA.

supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS BFA Program Net Monthly Income Limits (published 07/2026); FSM § 403 Resource Limits; FSM § 231.05 Expanded Categorical Eligibility Criteria
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: New Hampshire runs THREE parallel eligibility tracks — a plain 130%/100% FPG track with a $3,000 resource limit, a Target (elderly/disabled) track with a $4,500 resource limit, and an Expanded Categorically Eligible (ECE) track at 200% FPG gross income with NO resource test at all
supplements.text: New Hampshire DHHS's own current BFA Program Net Monthly Income Limits document (published 07/2026) lists three SNAP income columns by household size: the 130% FPG gross-income limit for households with no elderly/disabled member ($1,696 for household size 1), the 100% FPG net-income limit applicable to all households ($1,305), and a 200% FPG Expanded Categorical Eligibility (ECE) gross-income limit ($2,609). This pack reads New Hampshire's structure precisely rather than compressing it into a single flat "BBCE percentage" the way several secondary sources do: FSM § 231.05 defines ECE as available to a household whose gross income is ≤200% FPG AND who would receive or be eligible for a non-cash, MOE-funded service under Title IV-A (a threshold DHHS's own BFA Form 77u, Community Resources, is designed to satisfy) — ECE households are NOT subject to the SNAP resource test at all. A narrower "Categorically Eligible" pathway (households receiving TANF/FANF or SSI) is automatically resource-eligible as well. A household that is neither ECE- nor categorically-eligible falls into one of two remaining tracks: "Target" households (at least one member elderly, age 60+, or disabled) face a $4,500 resource limit, while "All Other" (Regular) households face a $3,000 resource limit — both groups also remain subject to the underlying 130%/100% FPG income tests. In practice, this pack's reading is that the large majority of NH SNAP households qualify via the 200% FPG ECE track and therefore never face a resource test at all, but a household that has not established ECE eligibility (or a Target household whose income exceeds 200% FPG) genuinely does face a real, enforced resource limit — this pack flags this precisely rather than asserting a flat "no asset limit in New Hampshire" claim the way several secondary sources this pack found do. One vehicle per adult household member is excluded as a resource regardless of value (He-W Chapter 741, 7 CFR 273.8(e)(3) baseline) — this pack did not independently fetch the full FSM § 409 Vehicles text and treats this specific figure as secondary-source corroborated only, see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS SR 97-27, dated 08/97, implementing HB 722-FN, Chapter 157, Laws of 1997, effective August 8, 1997 — full opt-out, no felony drug conviction restriction of any kind
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CONFIRMATION (of a minority-position claim): New Hampshire FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban in 1997 — this pack fetched the state's own 1997 implementing directive directly, not just secondary-source repetition
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found several secondary sources describing New Hampshire as having "fully opted out" of this federal provision — a claim this pack treats as a genuine minority position among states nationally (most states this roster has built carry a MODIFIED ban, not a full opt-out) that deserved primary-source confirmation rather than acceptance at face value. This pack fetched New Hampshire DHHS's own SR 97-27 (dated August 1997) directly and confirms the claim precisely: effective August 8, 1997, pursuant to House Bill 722-FN, Chapter 157, Laws of 1997, "an individual's felony drug conviction status is not taken into account for purposes of determining eligibility for TANF financial and/or medical assistance and food stamps. A convicted drug felon is eligible for TANF financial and/or medical assistance and food stamps provided all eligibility requirements are met." This is a genuine full opt-out — no treatment-program condition, no possession-vs-distribution distinction, no count-of-convictions threshold — and this pack found no subsequent SR reversing or narrowing SR 97-27's policy. This is distinct from New Hampshire's SEPARATE trafficking-related disqualification (an individual convicted of trading a controlled substance in exchange for SNAP benefits faces a 24-month disqualification for a first offense and permanent disqualification for a second), which is not a drug-felony-conviction ban but a program-integrity penalty tied specifically to using SNAP itself as trafficking currency — this pack flags the distinction explicitly so the two are not conflated.

supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS FSM Table I: SNAP Deductions — Standard Deduction $209 (household sizes 1-3), $223 (4), $261 (5), $299 (6+); Heating/Cooling SUA $1,018; Utilities-Only $373; Electric-Only $217; Telephone-Only $39; Excess Shelter Deduction $744; Homeless Shelter Deduction $199; He-W 742.02
supplements.heading: GENUINE STRUCTURAL DEPARTURE: New Hampshire's Heating/Cooling Standard Utility Allowance is $1,018/month — notably high — and its 4-tier utility structure includes a standalone "Electric-Only" tier distinct from a generic "Utilities-Only" tier
supplements.text: New Hampshire's Standard Deduction (per DHHS's current FSM Table I) is $209 for household sizes 1 through 3, $223 for size 4, $261 for size 5, and $299 for size 6 or more — matching the current national FFY2026 figures this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Kentucky, Louisiana, Alabama, and South Carolina packs have each independently confirmed. New Hampshire's utility-allowance structure is where this pack found a genuine, worth-flagging departure: unlike this roster's Nebraska (SUA/LUA/OUA/Telephone, four tiers split by qualifying-utility COUNT), New Hampshire's FSM Table I lists Heating/Cooling (A/C) at $1,018/month, Utilities-Only at $373, Electric-Only at $217, and Telephone-Only at $39 — four tiers, but split partly by utility TYPE rather than purely by count, with a standalone Electric-Only tier this pack did not find in any other state built in this roster so far. This pack flags the $1,018 Heating/Cooling figure explicitly as notably higher than the ~$600-750 range this roster's other cold-climate and non-cold-climate states alike have generally shown, consistent with New Hampshire's genuinely high regional heating-fuel costs, but recommends re-verifying this figure against a second DHHS source before treating it as beyond dispute — this pack's single Table I fetch is its only direct source for this specific number. Per DHHS's consumer SNAP page, only households with an elderly (60+) or disabled member can use a LIHEAP payment of more than $20/year to trigger automatic Heating/Cooling SUA eligibility — this pack flags this as a genuine NH-specific restriction on the common "heat and eat" LIHEAP-triggered SUA pathway, since several other states extend that automatic trigger to all household types rather than restricting it to elderly/disabled households only. New Hampshire's Medical Expense Deduction is a FLAT $135 standard shortcut — this pack flags this explicitly as a contrast to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Maryland, and Indiana packs, which use an actual-expense-only (no-shortcut) medical deduction mechanism; New Hampshire instead places with this roster's Kentucky, Louisiana, South Carolina, Missouri, Colorado, and Alabama packs' flat-shortcut camp. New Hampshire's Excess Shelter Deduction is $744/month (matching the current national FFY2026 figure this roster's other states have confirmed) and its Homeless Shelter Deduction is $199/month, close to but not identical to the $198.99 figure this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, and Louisiana packs cite — this pack reads the $1 difference as simple rounding in DHHS's own published table rather than a substantive New Hampshire-specific policy choice, but flags it for re-verification.

supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS FSM § 245.03 (current, post-11/1/2025 text) and § 245.05; USDA FNS/FNA ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index (no FY2026 New Hampshire entry)
supplements.heading: New Hampshire currently has NO active area-wide ABAWD waiver anywhere in the state — the state's prior Stratford/Hale's Location waiver expired 9/30/2025 and was not renewed
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month (3-year) period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched New Hampshire DHHS's own current FSM § 245.03 (Criteria for Exemption from ABAWD Work Requirements) directly via a live reader-proxy fetch — critically NOT relying on a stale Wayback Machine snapshot dated 10/31/2025, one day before the OBBBA changes took effect — and confirms the current, post-11/1/2025 exemption list: a household member under age 14 (narrowed from under 18), age 65 or older (a state-specific threshold, distinct from the federal ABAWD age-SCOPE ceiling of 64 that ends the work-requirement age range itself), pregnancy, residing in a high-unemployment area, being medically unfit for employment, and — a NEWLY ADDED exemption this pack flags explicitly — being an Indian, Urban Indian, California Indian, or other Indigenous individual eligible for Indian Health Services. Consistent with the OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effective 11/1/2025 in New Hampshire per DHHS's own consumer page) nationwide rollout this roster has documented in other 2025-2026-built packs, New Hampshire's ABAWD age scope expanded from 18-54 to 18-64, and the homeless, veteran, and former-foster-youth blanket exemptions were REMOVED — an applicant who previously understood themselves exempt on one of those bases, prior to 11/1/2025, is no longer exempt on that basis under current New Hampshire/federal law. This pack found and cross-checked: New Hampshire previously carried an area-wide ABAWD waiver covering the towns of Stratford and Hale's Location, which expired September 30, 2025 and was not renewed (WebSearch corroboration, not independently fetched); USDA FNS/FNA's own current ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index lists New Hampshire's most recent posted waiver-response entry as FY2025 (dated 09/03/2024), with no FY2026 entry — consistent with no currently active waiver anywhere in the state. New Hampshire's own FSM text includes "residing in certain areas with a high unemployment rate" as an exemption category in the abstract, but this pack found no evidence any New Hampshire location currently meets that threshold.

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA's current SNAP Restaurant Meals Program state list (New Hampshire absent); WebSearch corroboration (Propel, NH Food Bank)
supplements.heading: New Hampshire does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found consistent corroboration across DHHS's own consumer materials (which describe SNAP-eligible purchases as grocery-style food for home preparation and consumption, explicitly excluding "any 'hot' prepared foods that are ready to eat") and secondary sources (Propel's state EBT guide) that New Hampshire does NOT currently operate an RMP. This pack found no pending New Hampshire legislation analogous to Nebraska's LB920 that would establish one. New Hampshire's operative answer for an applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at a restaurant is a plain no — EBT purchases are limited to grocery-style items for home preparation, with the standard federal exceptions (SNAP Online Purchasing at Amazon, ALDI, Walmart, and several other retailers is available, but this is a grocery-delivery channel, not a restaurant-meals program).

supplements.citation: New Hampshire DHHS FSM § 133.09, Certification Periods; FSM § 161, Redetermination/Recertification — 36 months for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income (ESAP) households, 6 months for all other households
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FINDING: New Hampshire's STANDARD SNAP certification period is only 6 months — shorter than the 12-month norm most other states in this roster use — with a 36-month period reserved for ESAP households
supplements.text: New Hampshire DHHS's own current FSM § 133.09 (Certification Periods) states plainly and without qualification that SNAP certification periods are either 36 months (for households in which all adults are elderly or disabled and there is no earned income — the Elderly Simplified Application Project, ESAP, an FNS demonstration project DHHS implemented effective 07/01/2025) or 6 months (for all other households). This pack flags the 6-month standard period explicitly as a genuine structural departure worth naming: most of this roster's other states use a 12-month standard certification period for non-elderly/disabled households, with New Hampshire's 6-month period requiring roughly twice the recertification frequency for a working-age or earned-income household. Households recertified for a 6-month Simplified Reporting period are, per this pack's WebSearch corroboration (not independently fetched from a numbered FSM section), only required to report mid-period changes that cause gross monthly household income to exceed 130% FPG for the household size — a standard Simplified Reporting threshold-reporting rule, not full monthly reporting. ESAP households receive a yearly reminder to report any changes to expenses or deductions, with recertification conducted on paper or online unless the household requests an interview.
